planting.note: Plant a container-grown tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; as an all-male clone selected purely for sterile, pollen-bearing flowers, Stribling must be propagated by cuttings rather than seed and never sets fruit.

directions: Stribling was selected in California and introduced by Stribling Nursery in the early 1950s specifically as a seedless shade-tree alternative to fruiting mulberry seedlings. Its deeply lobed, glossy dark green leaves are larger than those of many other fruitless clones, and the tree develops into a broad, fast-growing, round-headed shade tree. Because it is an all-male selection, no berries ever form to drop and stain patios, walkways, or parked cars beneath it. Site it well away from paving to accommodate the wide-spreading surface roots, and prune while young to build strong scaffold branching.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Black Persian Mulberry (Large-Fruited True Black Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; true black mulberries are slower to establish than white mulberry selections, so stake young trees and water consistently through their first two summers.

directions: Black Persian is a true Morus nigra selection grown for unusually large fruit, often exceeding an inch long and nearly as wide, with juicy flesh and a rich, balanced subacid flavor more complex than most white mulberry cultivars. Like other black mulberries it grows more slowly into a dense, rounded tree and takes longer to reach bearing size than vigorous alba selections, rewarding the wait with long-lived, richly flavored fruit suited to fresh eating, wine, and preserves. Established trees handle drought reasonably well, though steady moisture during fruit swell improves berry size. Site it away from paving and parked cars, since the dark juice stains readily when ripe fruit drops.
sources: growables.org (University of Florida/CRFG archive) - Mulberry Cultivars

planting.note: Plant a dormant bare-root or containerized tree in early spring once the ground can be worked; Northrop's exceptional cold tolerance makes it one of the few named mulberry cultivars suited to short-season northern gardens, though young trees still benefit from a protective mulch through their first winters.

directions: Northrop traces to a single large mulberry tree planted in Potsdam, New York in the 1850s and was later propagated and distributed by St. Lawrence Nurseries as one of the hardiest named mulberry selections available in North America. The vigorous tree produces heavy crops of sweet, dark, blackberry-like fruit over an extended early- to mid-summer harvest window once established. Its primary value over most other named mulberry cultivars is sheer winter survival, reportedly tolerating cold that would kill less hardy selections outright. Give young trees a sheltered first few winters and expect some tip dieback in the coldest sites until the framework matures.
sources: Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association (MOFGA)

planting.note: Plant a dormant bare-root or rooted-cutting tree in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; River View was selected from vigorous Russian mulberry seedlings for its unusually heavy, consistent fruit set and tolerates poor or eroded soils better than most named cultivars once established.

directions: River View was picked out from a planting of hardy Russian mulberry seedlings growing above a cut riverbank, chosen for standing out among its siblings as the most dependably heavy-bearing tree in the group. It carries the classic toughness of Russian-strain white mulberry, shrugging off poor, rocky, or eroded soils and extended dry spells with little supplemental irrigation once established. Fruit is medium-small, black, and sweetly flavored, ripening over the long summer season typical of white mulberry seedlings. Because unselected Russian mulberry seedlings vary widely in fruit quality, a named selection like River View offers more predictable flavor and yield for a home orchard.

common_name: Rupp's Romanian Mulberry (Hardy Sweet Black Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting or small container tree in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Rupp's Romanian is slow to reach full size but adapts to a wide range of soils once established.

directions: Rupp's Romanian descends from a chance seedling grown from mulberry stock imported from Romania in the 1940s and was later named and propagated for its combination of cold hardiness and fruit quality. The tree is notably slower-growing than most named mulberry selections but tolerates a wider range of soils and more shade than faster, more demanding cultivars. Nearly seedless, glossy black fruit ripens over an unusually long cropping season, with flavor often compared to Illinois Everbearing but a touch sweeter and more delicate. Its cold tolerance into zone 4 makes it a useful option for northern growers wanting fruit quality closer to that of the better-known hybrid selections.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
